name: hCG
lead: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is a hormone made by the placenta that resembles luteinizing hormone (LH). It can trigger ovulation in women and stimulate testosterone production in the testes [1]. Pharmaceutical hCG is prescription-only and is made either from the urine of pregnant women or by recombinant DNA technology [1].

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities hCG is discussed mainly by men who use testosterone or anabolic steroids. They say it keeps the testes working while the body's own signal from the pituitary is suppressed, which in their account helps maintain testicular size, fertility and hormonal balance during and after cycles, and so supports the physique and masculine-looking development they are working toward [2][3]. Some posters also discuss it alongside growth hormone or other compounds for facial or bone changes; no studies were found testing hCG for those outcomes [8].

The hormone has three public identities: a pregnancy-test marker (the beta subunit is what home tests detect), a fertility and hypogonadism medicine, and the subject of the 1950s Simeons weight-loss protocol that regulators later acted against.[1][14] In sport it is on some banned-substance lists because it raises testosterone in men.[1]

In medicine hCG is used to treat some forms of male hypogonadism, to induce ovulation and support fertility treatment, and, through its beta subunit, as a tumor marker [1][4]. A 2014 review of anabolic-steroid-induced hypogonadism lists hCG among the options clinicians use when managing men whose own testosterone production has been suppressed by steroid use [9]. The FDA has described over-the-counter hCG weight-loss products as fraudulent [1].

chain: Keeps Leydig cells producing testosterone and testicular volume during exogenous androgen use
Supports hormonal function and fertility alongside a testosterone regimen
angle.text: Men on testosterone regimens use hCG to keep the testes stimulated while the pituitary signal is switched off. Practitioners describe this as maintaining natural testosterone output and testicular size, which they link to a steadier hormonal environment for training and body composition. It has no direct action on the face or skin.

infobox: Glycoprotein, 237 amino acids; alpha and beta subunits [1]

paras: In fertility treatment, ovulation occurs about 38 to 40 hours after a single hCG injection, and IVF patients typically receive it to trigger ovulation, with egg retrieval scheduled about 34 to 36 hours later [1]. hCG is also used to support the corpus luteum and boost progesterone production in certain circumstances [1].

In men, hCG stimulates Leydig cells to produce testosterone, and the resulting intratesticular testosterone is needed for sperm production [1]. It is used for some types of hypogonadism, either alone or more commonly together with testosterone, and to treat or prevent infertility, for example during testosterone replacement therapy [1][4]. It does not work when the testes themselves cannot make testosterone [4]. A 2024 systematic review of gonadotropins for inducing puberty in males with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism covered 103 studies and 5,328 patients; hCG was the gonadotropin used in 93 of the studies [16].

Because its beta subunit is secreted by some cancers, including seminoma and choriocarcinoma, hCG is also measured as a tumor marker. Combined with alpha-fetoprotein it is used to monitor germ cell tumors [1]. Pregnancy tests detect hCG with antibodies specific to the beta subunit [1].

Forum users on looksmax.org say hCG is started alongside testosterone to prevent testicular atrophy, since signaling from the pituitary declines once exogenous testosterone is introduced [3]. Others describe it as optional for lower-dose regimens, adding it if budget allows [2]. Anabolic steroids suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, and reference sources confirm that users take hCG during and after cycles to mimic LH [1].

A separate thread suggests that people who take large amounts of growth hormone for bone or facial growth should look into hCG; the original poster argued that raising testosterone would matter more than increasing the growth hormone amount, and other users disputed the reasoning [8]. T Nation forum members discuss hCG mainly in the context of testosterone replacement therapy, including fertility goals and whether to add it to a prescribed protocol [10][11]. Some members report buying it through channels outside prescription, which is how the gray market for the drug is described there [12].

For its established medical purposes the evidence base is large. Reviews of male hypogonadotropic hypogonadism describe gonadotropin therapy as the approach that promotes testicular growth and spermatogenesis, whereas testosterone alone promotes virilization but not testicular growth or sperm production [16]. The 2014 review of steroid-associated hypogonadism notes that no studies of high enough quality could be pooled, and presents management using testosterone, hCG and selective estrogen receptor modulators as expert-opinion-based [9].

Forum members who use hCG report that it helps testicular size and subjective wellbeing; a T Nation poster described feeling worse after stopping it, while another reported a weight increase and mood changes after stopping both an aromatase inhibitor and hCG [11][13]. These are individual accounts, and no trial has tested hCG for appearance outcomes.

hCG is a glycoprotein of 237 amino acids with a molecular mass of about 36.7 kDa. It is made of an alpha subunit shared with LH, FSH and TSH and a beta subunit unique to hCG [1]. A carboxy-terminal peptide on the beta subunit gives it a longer half-life than LH [1].

It binds the LH/hCG receptor. In the ovary this maintains the corpus luteum during early pregnancy; in the testes it stimulates Leydig cells to synthesize testosterone [1]. Humans make several forms, including regular hCG, hyperglycosylated hCG and a free beta subunit, each with different physiological roles [1].

Pregnyl, Novarel, Profasi, Pubergen, Choragon and Follutein are extracted from the urine of pregnant women, while Ovidrel is made with recombinant DNA technology [1]. Two registered trials compared the urinary and recombinant forms or tested recombinant hCG for final follicle maturation in IVF [5][6].

Reference warnings for women include ectopic pregnancy, multiple pregnancy, pregnancy loss and thromboembolism. In men, prolonged use can increase androgen production, and caution applies in prepubescent teenagers because of the risk of precocious puberty or premature epiphyseal closure [1].

Because it raises testicular testosterone output, hCG also raises estradiol through aromatization. Forum users who add it to a testosterone regimen describe pairing it with an aromatase inhibitor for that reason [8]; the clinical literature on steroid-associated hypogonadism describes combining hCG with other agents under medical supervision [9].

The international unit of hCG was first established in 1938 and redefined in 1964 and 1980.[1] Urinary preparations were the original pharmaceutical form, and recombinant hCG (Ovidrel) later joined them.[1] Pregnancy tests work by detecting the beta subunit with specific antibodies, with urine tests detecting from about 20 to 100 mIU/mL depending on brand and serum tests as low as 5 mIU/mL.[1]

Albert T. W. Simeons (1900 to 1970), a British endocrinologist who studied at Heidelberg and died in Rome, became the leading advocate of hCG for weight loss.[23] He published the book Pounds and Inches and a related paper in The Lancet in 1954, proposing daily hCG injections with a very-low-calorie diet of about 500 calories; he said he had observed fat loss without muscle loss in calorie-restricted pregnant women in India and in obese boys with pituitary problems given low-dose hCG.[14][1] His other books included Man's Presumptuous Brain (1961) and Food: Facts, Foibles and Fables (1968).[23]

That protocol became the best-known public association with the drug and the origin of the term hCG diet. Its use among men on anabolic steroids is a separate tradition from bodybuilding, where hCG has been discussed as a way to restart or maintain testicular function around cycles.[1][9]

In 1976 a double-blind study in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition found hCG no more effective than dietary restriction alone, and the FDA required Simeons and others to add a disclaimer to hCG obesity advertising stating it was not approved as safe and effective for obesity.[14][1] A 1995 meta-analysis by Lijesen and colleagues rated the supporting studies as methodologically poor and concluded there was no scientific evidence that hCG causes weight loss, fat redistribution or reduced hunger; the American Society of Bariatric Physicians is quoted by Wikipedia as saying no new clinical trials have been published since.[1][14]

The diet returned to public attention in the late 2000s. In 2008 the FTC barred the marketer Kevin Trudeau from making hCG diet claims, and he was later jailed over violating a court order.[14] Injectable hCG faced a shortage in 2010, in January 2011 the FDA called over-the-counter hCG products fraudulent, and on 6 December 2011 the FDA and FTC moved against unapproved and homeopathic hCG weight-loss products; some suppliers then sold so-called hormone-free versions built around amino acids or claims of radionic energy transfer.[14] Wikipedia says the diets typically prescribe 500 to 1,000 calories a day and that the scientific consensus attributes any weight loss to the severe calorie restriction, with malnutrition risk; on 15 November 2016 the American Medical Association adopted a policy that using hCG for weight loss is inappropriate.[14][1]

hCG is on some sports' banned-substance lists, since it raises testosterone in men.[1] Wikipedia lists sanctions including Major League Baseball's Manny Ramirez (a 50-game ban in 2009), the NFL's Brian Cushing (a four-game ban after a positive urine test, reported in 2010), UFC's Dennis Siver (a fine of $19,800 and nine-month suspension reported in 2014) and Jurickson Profar (an 80-game suspension in 2025).[1]

In the United States hCG is available only by prescription. Forum posts show that some users obtain it without a prescription, including from overseas pharmacies [12][15]. Some T Nation posters say their physicians will prescribe testosterone but not hCG [15].

Anabolic steroids suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis in a dose-dependent way, which can cause androgen-induced hypogonadism, testicular atrophy, reduced sperm production and infertility; Wikipedia's steroid article lists hCG, alongside clomifene, among therapies used to restore testicular function after use.[24] Reference sources say hCG is commonly used during and after steroid cycles to maintain testicular size and testosterone production.[1] Anabolic steroids are Schedule III in the United States and many other countries, while hCG itself is prescription-only.[24]

The 2014 review of steroid-induced hypogonadism describes combinations of testosterone, hCG and selective estrogen receptor modulators for clinicians and notes the evidence is largely expert opinion.[9] Within communities, users discuss hCG as a recovery and maintenance tool rather than as a muscle-building drug in itself.

Registered trials include recombinant hCG for final follicle maturation in Chinese women undergoing IVF (NCT01081756, n=218, phase 3, started 2003), urinary versus recombinant hCG on oocyte maturity (NCT01507376, n=180, phase 3, started 2010), and hormonal stimulation of spermatogenesis in men with non-obstructive azoospermia (NCT05483621, n=100, phase 1, started 2021) [5][6][7]. Other registered trials examine low-dose hCG to reduce ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome and intrauterine hCG flushing on ICSI outcome [17][18].

A 2024 randomized, double-blind trial tested sublingual hCG as an adjuvant to ovulation induction with clomiphene or letrozole and found no statistically significant difference in ovulation induction between groups [19]. A 2024 randomized trial examined luteal hCG supplementation in GnRH-agonist-triggered fresh embryo transfer cycles [20]. The 2024 systematic review of gonadotropins for pubertal induction in males with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is the largest synthesis of male hCG use [16].
No studies were found of hCG for facial appearance, height or muscle outcomes in men using testosterone.

lore.intro: hCG is discussed as an accessory to testosterone regimens and sometimes as a standalone testosterone raiser or a companion to growth hormone [3][8].

claims.claim: hCG prevents testicular atrophy during testosterone use
claims.believers: Posters say hCG mimics LH so the testes keep working while exogenous testosterone suppresses the pituitary, and that it is best started when the natural signal starts to decline [3].
claims.experts: Reference sources report hCG helps preserve fertility and prevent testicular atrophy during testosterone replacement [1][4].

claims.claim: hCG is not essential for a low-dose first cycle
claims.believers: One user said it was not needed at a lower dose but worth adding if finances allow [2].
claims.experts: No published studies were found addressing this community question.

claims.claim: hCG helps facial growth in people taking growth hormone
claims.believers: One looksmax.org poster said hCG probably does more for facial growth than raising growth hormone from a lower to a higher amount, and that it keeps blood sugar from rising; other users challenged the blood sugar point [8].
claims.experts: No published studies were found testing hCG for facial or bone growth in this setting. Reference sources note that in adolescents hCG carries a risk of premature epiphyseal closure [1].

claims.claim: hCG lets men on testosterone keep fertility
claims.believers: A T Nation member said hCG helped him become fertile enough to have two children after hypogonadism [21].
claims.experts: Medical sources describe hCG as used to treat or prevent infertility in men, including during testosterone therapy [1][16].

claims.claim: Testosterone suspension removes the need for hCG
claims.believers: A T Nation post quoted a study excerpt reporting that testosterone suspension upregulates Leydig cell IGF receptors and prevents atrophy [22].
claims.experts: Clinical sources describe hCG as the standard add-on to preserve testicular function during androgen therapy [1][9]; this specific claim has not been examined.

claims.claim: The hCG diet melts fat without muscle loss
claims.believers: Simeons proposed that low-dose hCG with a roughly 500-calorie diet redistributed fat while sparing muscle, and revival marketing in the 2000s repeated the idea.[14][23]
claims.experts: A 1976 double-blind study found no advantage over diet alone, a 1995 meta-analysis found no scientific evidence of weight loss from hCG, the FDA called over-the-counter products fraudulent in 2011 and the AMA called weight-loss use inappropriate in 2016.[14][1]

claims.claim: hCG raises estrogen and needs to be paired with an aromatase inhibitor
claims.believers: Posters who add hCG to testosterone say the extra testicular output aromatizes to estradiol, so they pair it with an aromatase inhibitor.[8]
claims.experts: Reference sources say hCG raises androgen production in men, and the steroid-hypogonadism literature describes combinations of agents under medical supervision.[1][9]

claims.claim: hCG is banned in sport because it acts like a steroid
claims.believers: Athletes and forum members say it keeps testosterone production up during cycles.[3]
claims.experts: Because hCG raises testosterone in men it is on some sports' banned lists, and MLB, NFL and UFC athletes have been sanctioned.[1]

claims.claim: hCG over the counter can be bought online
claims.believers: T Nation posters describe getting hCG from overseas online pharmacies without a prescription.[12][15]
claims.experts: In the United States hCG is prescription-only, and the FDA and FTC acted against unapproved hCG products in 2011.[1][14]

card.summary: An LH-mimicking Rx hormone used with testosterone to keep the testes active; established in medicine, unstudied for looks.
card.note: Prescription-only; banned in sport; OTC weight-loss products have been called fraudulent by the FDA.

quick.overview:
hCG is a pregnancy hormone that imitates LH. Medically it triggers ovulation and treats some male hypogonadism.

In forums, men on testosterone use it to keep testicles functioning. No studies were found on appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: It binds the LH receptor, prompting the ovary or testes to produce sex hormones, including testosterone from Leydig cells.
quick.risks: Reference warnings include thromboembolism and multiple pregnancy in women, and precocious puberty risk in prepubescent teenagers. Prescription-only in the US and banned in several sports.
